articles.title: Substrate energetics in non-templated DNA synthesis by terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase
articles.abstract: Abstract DNA polymerases typically use deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) for DNA synthesis, yet the contribution of the γ-phosphate to catalysis remains unclear. Here, we examine the role of substrate energetics in enzyme-catalyzed polymerization using a fidelity-independent model polymerase, terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT). Relative to dNTPs, we find that TdT utilizes the canonical deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (dNDPs) with reduced rates and catalytic efficiencies, but diminished substrate bias. This lower specificity indicates that the γ-phosphate contributes primarily to nucleotide discrimination, rather than phosphodiester bond formation. Furthermore, our work shows that dNDPs and dNTPs with the same nucleobase exhibit comparable activation energies for the rate-limiting step during DNA synthesis, supporting a model in which the γ-phosphate is not required for lowering the energetic barrier for TdT-catalyzed polymerization. These findings define a mechanistic framework for understanding non-templated DNA synthesis and its application in enzymatic DNA synthesis technologies.

articles.title: Biosynthetic allene and alkyne formation by enzymatic prenyl demethylation
articles.abstract: Abstract Allenes and alkynes are versatile functional groups in chemical biology and drug discovery. However, how nature biosynthetically installs them in natural products, especially allenes, remains poorly understood. Here we uncovered that allenes and alkynes can be formed enzymatically through oxidative C( sp 2 )-demethylation of the common five-carbon prenyl group. Two fungal cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, PpnB and NseB, from the penipratynolene and sinuxylamide biosynthetic pathways, respectively, were shown to catalyze oxidative removal of a C( sp 2 )-methyl group in O -prenyl l -tyrosine to afford O -homoallenyl l -tyrosine and O -but-2-ynyl l -tyrosine, respectively. Combining density functional theory calculations and biochemical assays with isotopically labeled substrates, a mechanism involving selective C–C bond cleavage followed by product-determining hydrogen atom abstraction is presented. An additional P450 enzyme from the penipratynolene pathway, PpnD, acts as an oxidative isomerase that converts the four-carbon terminal allene into a terminal alkyne. This sophisticated enzymatic editing strategy to install allene and alkyne expands the catalytic repertoire of P450 enzymes.
articles.authors: Mengting Liu · Masao Ohashi · Wenyu Han

articles.title: Chemical Inhibition of Pyocyanin Biosynthesis Attenuates Virulence of Pseudomonas aeruginosa
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Anti‐virulence strategies that disarm bacterial pathogenicity without affecting viability offer a promising alternative to traditional antibiotics by reducing selective pressure for resistance. However, in Gram‐negative bacteria such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa , the double‐layered cell envelope limits intracellular access of small‐molecule inhibitors. Here, we screened a structurally diverse library of virulence inhibitors, previously established as pathoblockers in Gram‐positive bacteria, and identified a potent β‐lactone inhibitor of pyocyanin production. Activity‐based protein profiling revealed PqsC, an intracellular enzyme involved in Pseudomonas quinolone signal (PQS) quorum sensing, as the primary molecular target. Accordingly, global proteomic analysis revealed widespread dysregulation of enzymes associated with the pyocyanin biosynthetic pathway. Biochemical assays confirmed inhibition of recombinant PqsBC, while intact protein mass spectrometry and site‐directed mutagenesis established active site Cys129 as the covalent binding site. X‐ray crystallography of the inhibited complex revealed a covalent binding mode. Subsequent virtual screening identified a chloroacetamide scaffold that exhibited enhanced potency and a well‐defined binding mode. Importantly, supernatants from treated bacterial cultures showed reduced cytotoxicity toward mammalian cells, consistent with attenuated virulence. Collectively, this study identifies novel covalent inhibitors of PqsC and provides a mechanistic framework for the development of pathoblockers against P. aeruginosa .
articles.authors: Wei Ding · Sebastian R. Borgert · Wulf Blankenfeldt

articles.title: Natural product biosynthesis by guanidine prenyltransferases in plants and bacteria
articles.abstract: Guanidine exists almost exclusively as a resonance-stabilized cation, making its direct enzymatic functionalization challenging. We identified the cyanobacterial enzyme NosH, which catalyzes direct prenyl transfer to free guanidine. Structural and mechanistic analyses revealed guanidine activation by a two-aspartate clamp coupled to prenyl-donor binding through a distinct catalytic architecture. Guided by these features, we identified a large family of guanidine prenyltransferases across bacteria and plants. Plant enzymes produced guanidine alkaloids such as galegine in vitro and heterologous expression of a plant ortholog in Nicotiana benthamiana produced galegine in planta, providing a direct enzymatic link to plant-specialized metabolism.

articles.title: Nitrene generation and transfer for unnatural biosynthesis in living cells
articles.abstract: Abstract Synthetic biology has enabled the production of natural and unnatural products from inexpensive sustainable feedstocks. Yet, the scope of available products has been limited largely to compounds accessible from nature’s chemical reactions. Evolved enzymes can catalyse reactions of unnatural substrates or reactions not found in nature but often require the addition of synthetic reagents to purified enzymes or to resting cells containing those enzymes. Here we show that chemical reactions of metabolic intermediates produced intracellularly in living cells can include intermolecular nitrene transfers. The biosynthesis of N -acetoxyanilines, in combination with the generation and transfer of N -aryl nitrene intermediates from them catalysed by a cytochrome P450, generates amino alcohols, diamines, diarylamines and aminoalkyl arenes from simple carbon feedstocks. These products—common substructures of pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals—are challenging to synthesize by standard organic chemistry and were produced from inexpensive, renewable feedstocks. Evolution of the enzymes in this pathway showed that titres can be increased by engineering and that the products can be synthesized with high enantioselectivity.

articles.title: Protein Scaffolds Modulate the Electronic Structure of a Common Ketyl Radical Intermediate in Thiamine Pyrophosphate-Dependent Radical Biocatalysis: Insights from EPR and ENDOR Spectroscopy
articles.abstract: Abstract New-to-nature radical biocatalysis has emerged as a powerful strategy for asymmetric C–C bond formation, yet the enzyme-bound radical intermediates that underpin these transformations have remained largely uncharacterized. Here, we combine photobiocatalytic reaction development with multifrequency electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), electron–nuclear double resonance (ENDOR) spectroscopy, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to elucidate the ketyl radical intermediates formed during thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)-dependent radical biocatalysis. We first develop an oxidative photobiocatalytic cross-coupling of aldehydes with alkyltrifluoroborates catalyzed by engineered benzoylformate decarboxylase (BFD) variants, providing enantioenriched α-chiral ketones through a new oxidative radical manifold inaccessible to benzaldehyde lyases (BALs). Freeze-quench multifrequency EPR and ENDOR spectroscopy directly identify the catalytically generated TPP-bound ketyl radical and reveal that this common radical intermediate adopts distinct electronic structures in BFD and BAL despite their identical chemical composition. Analysis of 1H, 19F, 31P, and 14N hyperfine interactions, together with DFT calculations, demonstrates that enzyme-specific active-site conformations redistribute spin density between the TPP cofactor and substrate fragment. Greater substrate-centered spin delocalization in BFD provides a mechanistic basis for its superior radical C–C coupling activity relative to BAL. These results establish a direct relationship between protein-controlled electronic structure and catalytic function in TPP-dependent radical biocatalysis and demonstrate that engineering the electronic properties of a common radical intermediate represents a useful strategy for controlling enzyme reactivity in radical biocatalysis.
articles.authors: Guodong Rao · Zheng Zhang · Xin Liu

articles.title: Decentralized Biosynthesis of the Spiro-DKP Alkaloid Chevalinulin A Enabled by Nonclustered P450 and Intermolecular [4 + 2] Cyclase
articles.abstract: Abstract Intermolecular Diels–Alder (DA) cycloadditions are pivotal for constructing complex polycyclic architectures. However, biological catalysts performing this transformation on diketopiperazine (DKP) cores remain largely unidentified. Here, we report a decentralized biosynthetic pathway in the deep-sea cold-seep sourced fungus Aspergillus chevalieri CS-122 that assembles chevalinulin A, a spiro[bicyclo[2.2.2]octane]-DKP alkaloid. This pathway involves two nonclustered enzymes, CalO and FadA. CalO is a cytochrome P450 that furnishes an essential exocyclic olefin, while FadA represents the first FAD oxidoreductase-like Diels–Alderase that catalyzes an intermolecular, endoselective [4 + 2] cycloaddition between neoechinulin B and 3,4-trans-cyclohexadiene. These enzymes function downstream of a conserved gene cluster, effectively decoupling core scaffold assembly from late-stage functionalization. This strategy likely underpins the extensive structural diversity of fungal DKP alkaloids. Notably, CalO and FadA were identified via an integrated transcriptomic and structure-guided computational pipeline, rather than sequence homology, demonstrating the efficacy of this approach in mining functional catalysts from genomic “dark matter”. Mutational analysis indicates that residues M193, Y226, Y315, and D446 are critical in FadA activity. This study reveals a decentralized biosynthetic paradigm linking clustered core assembly with dispersed diversification, establishing a general framework for engineering complex alkaloid scaffolds.
articles.authors: Ling-Hong Meng · Li-Yao Wang · Zhen Ying
